rejected.title: Trench warfare on the Western Front
card: The Western Front was the line of fighting across France and Belgium. From late 1914, both sides dug long lines of trenches to shelter from enemy fire.
The ground between the opposing trenches was called no man's land. Soldiers who attacked had to cross it in the open.
Machine guns could fire many bullets a minute at advancing soldiers. Artillery shelled both trenches and open ground, and gas could drift into trenches.
Defenders in trenches had cover, while attackers had none. So attacks often cost many lives and gained little ground.
rejected.remember: Weapons favoured defenders in trenches, so crossing no man's land was deadly.

a.q: Why were attacks across no man's land so costly?
opts: Attackers crossed open ground under heavy enemy fire
Attackers had no weapons and could only run at the enemy
Defenders left their trenches and met attackers in the open
Gas was the only weapon used by either side
a.why: Attackers had to cross open ground while defenders fired from cover with machine guns and artillery. Gas was one danger among several, so it was not the only cause of losses.
a.clue: Think about who had cover and who did not.

b.q: A battalion attacks across no man's land toward enemy trenches on the Western Front. Which is the most likely result?
opts: Heavy losses for little gain in ground
A quick advance because the defenders had cover
Few losses because machine guns were rarely used
An easy win because attackers sheltered in trenches
b.why: Defenders in trenches had machine guns and artillery, while attackers crossed open ground. This usually meant heavy losses and little ground gained. Having cover helped the defenders, not the attackers.
b.clue: Who was exposed while crossing the open ground?

version.title: Trench warfare on the Western Front
card: The Western Front was a line of fighting across Belgium and France. From late 1914 both sides dug long lines of trenches facing each other, protected by barbed wire.
The open ground between the two lines of trenches was called no man's land. To attack, soldiers had to climb out and cross it.
Machine guns could fire hundreds of bullets a minute. Artillery fired shells from kilometres away, and poison gas could choke or blind soldiers.
Defenders could shelter in their trenches while attackers were in the open. So attacks often cost thousands of lives and gained little ground.
version.remember: Trenches and new weapons made defending easier than attacking, so attacks cost many lives for little gain.

a.q: Why did trenches give defenders an advantage on the Western Front?
opts: They sheltered defenders while attackers were exposed
They let defenders advance quickly across no man's land
They stopped artillery shells from being fired at all
They kept poison gas out of every part of the line
a.why: Trenches let defenders shelter from bullets and shells, while attackers crossing no man's land had no cover. Advancing quickly is the reverse: trenches made fast advances hard.
a.clue: Who was in the open during an attack?

b.q: A general orders an attack across no man's land in daylight. The enemy's barbed wire is still uncut, and its machine guns are ready. What is the most likely result?
opts: Heavy losses and very little ground taken
A fast advance, as the attackers have cover
Few losses, as machine guns fire too slowly
A big gain, as defenders leave their trenches
b.why: Uncut wire slows attackers in the open while ready machine guns fire on them, so heavy losses for little ground is most likely. Cover helped the defenders, not the attackers crossing no man's land.
b.clue: Who has cover, and who is in the open?

a.best: They sheltered defenders while attackers were exposed

b.best: Heavy losses and very little ground taken
